narrative: The model estimated a 46% probability that you will leave your job—a near one-in-two risk—and that risk is why the promotion was denied. In effect, the organization judged that promoting you now could be wasted if you exit soon. Your strongest signal was your total years of experience, and it actually worked in your favor: having 1–5 years is common among employees predicted to stay, so this lowered the leave risk. The more concerning factor was that you reported other job opportunities while in this role. Among employees predicted to stay, only about a quarter had such opportunities, so this pushed the model toward leaving. Your sector—“other”—also modestly increased the leave risk compared with sectors where stayers are more concentrated. So the model saw your external options and sector context as retention warning signs, even though your early-career experience counted as stabilizing. Before reconsidering promotion, the organization should discuss your career path, recognition, workload, pay and benefits, and whether your role can offer clearer growth; you should clarify what would keep you engaged. A promotion decision should not rest only on a leave-risk estimate, but this risk should prompt a retention conversation and a concrete development plan.
